meta.blurb: Kofi has wanted to make pottery for years, and nothing has happened. His neighbour Ana, a retired mountain guide, says a wish with no date is only a wish. So he sets one. Twenty mugs, sold by the end of June.
meta.bible: Kofi Mensah: a twenty-nine-year-old accountant who dreams of making Pottery; thoughtful, careful with numbers, afraid of looking foolish. Ana Silva: his neighbour, sixty-six, a retired mountain guide of thirty years, plain-spoken and kind; she turns groups back when the weather is bad. Joy Bell: the teacher of a beginners' class at the community Studio, cheerful and honest. Dan: Kofi's friend. Riverside Market: the town market where Kofi sells on the last Saturday of June. The goal: sell twenty Mugs that Kofi made himself before the thirtieth of June, about twenty-six weeks from the first of January; he sells sixteen. Five hours a week: Tuesday and Thursday evenings and Saturday morning. Key terms: Wish, Goal, Deadline, Milestone, Clay, Glaze, Kiln, Wheel, Tally, Obstacle, Review. Real research, mentioned carefully: psychologists have found over several decades that specific, challenging goals tend to bring better results than vague ones; plans in an if-then form have helped many people follow through; imagining obstacles as well as success may help in some studies; the effect of telling others about a goal is mixed. No other studies or numbers are invented. This is original practical self-help for adults, one idea in each beat, building to a final takeaway. Voice and tone: warm, concrete, encouraging, never bossy. Added cast: Abena: Kofi's older sister, a nurse, warm and teasing. Priya: Kofi's colleague at the accounting firm, sharp and generous. Tomas: a retired baker of seventy in Kofi's class, patient with clay. Lena: a young art student in the class, quick and cheerful. Rosa Quinn: the organiser of Riverside Market. Hannah: a potter who sells at the next stall in the market. Joy teaches beginners on Thursday evenings from six to eight, and the Studio opens for practice on Tuesday evenings and Saturday mornings. Kofi's flat is on the second floor; Ana's is on the first, above a courtyard with her pots of herbs. Prices and money: each mug costs eighteen pounds. Kofi sells five mugs before the market (to Dan, Priya, Abena and Tomas) and eleven at the market, sixteen in all. A cracked batch in the kiln costs him four mugs. About twenty-five good mugs are made in all; twenty go to the market. His next goal: sell forty mugs by the end of December, with a small online page. Added terms: Wedging, Centring, Throwing, Handle, Trimming, Tarp, Batch, Check-in, Review, Stall, Float, Tile. The story runs from the first of January to the thirtieth of June, then on to a warm evening in late summer; the year is not named. Priya, Abena, Tomas, Lena, Hannah and Rosa Quinn are all minor characters; Dan is Kofi's friend. Ana's own wish is to walk a long coastal path.

beats.summary: The busy season begins at work, and Kofi stays late and misses his Tuesday session.

beats.scene: Kofi lies under a blanket with a cup of tea

beats.summary: Kofi wants to give up, but Ana arrives with soup and says never miss twice in a row.

beats.scene: Kofi colours a dot on the mirror chart beside an empty gap
beats.summary: Kofi leaves the gap in his chart instead of hiding it, and the next dot is a small victory.

beats.scene: Kofi puts his two charts on a table in front of Ana

beats.scene: Kofi tells his friend Dan about his plan over dinner

beats.summary: Dan teases but offers to be Kofi's first customer, and Kofi decides to tell only people who will ask how it goes.

beats.scene: Priya leans over her desk to look at a photo of a mug
beats.summary: Priya asks to see a photo of the first mug at work and says to put her down for one.

beats.scene: Kofi sets up a small table and a covered clay bucket in his flat
beats.summary: Kofi makes the first step easy by setting up a small work corner at home.

beats.scene: Kofi puts his phone in a drawer and a sketchbook on the table

beats.scene: Kofi closes a laptop showing a language course beside a pottery sketchbook
beats.summary: A new, interesting idea tempts Kofi, a Spanish course, and he decides to park it until after June.

beats.scene: Kofi writes After June at the top of a page in a notebook
beats.summary: Kofi opens an After June page in his notebook for new ideas, and feels relieved.

beats.scene: Kofi writes three lines in a notebook on a Sunday evening
beats.summary: Kofi starts a weekly review: what went well, what got in the way, and the next three steps.

beats.scene: Kofi writes a line in his notebook beside a mug of tea
beats.summary: In his first review, Kofi writes what went well: he pulled the walls up without a collapse.

beats.scene: Kofi frowns at his notebook, the second heading underlined twice
beats.summary: Kofi writes what got in the way: he stayed late at work on Tuesday and arrived at the Studio tired.

beats.summary: Kofi writes three clear steps for the coming week, each small enough to finish.

beats.summary: Kofi tests green glaze on small tiles first, so that a mistake costs a little clay and not a whole mug.

beats.scene: Kofi holds two tiles, one blue and one green, up to the window light
beats.summary: Kofi chooses blue and green, and notes why on a card: they look warm and sell well in a plain kitchen.

beats.scene: Kofi circles the word Tuesday in his notebook with a thick pen
beats.summary: Reading his reviews, Kofi sees that Tuesdays are always the weakest, and he changes his plan.

beats.scene: Kofi reads a pile of old notebook pages on his bed
beats.summary: Reading six weeks of reviews, Kofi sees real progress he had missed from day to day.

beats.scene: Kofi pulls a handle from a strip of soft clay with wet fingers
beats.summary: Handles are the next hardest part, so Kofi practises pulling them, one after another.

beats.scene: Ana and Kofi look at a calendar with the first of April circled
beats.summary: Ana points out that the halfway camp is close, so it is time for an honest look at the whole plan.

beats.summary: On the first of April, at the halfway point, Kofi and Ana sit by the river and look at everything.

beats.summary: Ana asks Kofi whether the goal still feels right, and whether he would choose it again today.

beats.summary: The numbers show Kofi is behind: seven mugs are finished, and he had hoped for ten by now.

beats.scene: Kofi looks down at the grass with his hands on his knees
beats.summary: Kofi's first thought is to give up the date, but Ana says: change the plan, not the goal.

beats.summary: Kofi counts what he needs: twenty-three more mugs in six weeks, which is about four every week.

beats.summary: Kofi makes a weekly target for his work: throw six mugs a week and keep at least four.

beats.scene: Kofi redraws his timeline with a new line added to the wall chart
beats.summary: Kofi redraws his timeline, moving the dates of his work but leaving the finish on the thirtieth of June.

beats.scene: Kofi walks home under falling blossom with a folded plan in his hand
beats.summary: Kofi leaves the check-in with one decision, to work in batches, and walks home under falling blossom.

beats.summary: Kofi keeps a sheet called Lessons: thin bottoms, slow drying, small experiments, and no hurry in the kiln.

beats.summary: After a bad Thursday, when three mugs collapse, Kofi feels like quitting, and he lies awake.

beats.summary: When he feels like quitting, Kofi rereads his reason on the card and decides to keep going.

beats.summary: Kofi takes Dan to dinner to celebrate ten good mugs, because small rewards keep effort alive.

beats.summary: Dan asks how much a mug costs, and Kofi realises he has never thought about a price.

On the shelf above his desk sits a pottery book that Kofi bought three years ago. Next to it is a lump of clay that has dried out and cracked like an old stone.

On the morning of the first of January, Kofi walks into the courtyard and finds Ana Silva repotting her herbs. She is sixty-six, a retired mountain guide, and she asks him what he wants from the new year.
Kofi hears himself say that he has always wanted to make pottery, and that he will do it someday. Ana smiles and says that someday is a fine word for a wish, but not for a goal.
Ana draws a cloud on a piece of paper and a small flag on a hill beside it. A wish is like the cloud, she says, but a goal is like the flag, because you can walk to it.
Ana tells Kofi that in thirty years she never guided a trip that began with the words someday or maybe. Every journey began with a date, a route and a plan written on paper.
Ana says that wishes stay wishes for three reasons. They have no date, they have no first step, and they ask nothing of you today.
Kofi thinks back over the last five years of his life. He has talked about pottery, bought a book and watched videos, but he has never once touched clay.
Ana offers Kofi a simple deal for the rest of the afternoon. If he comes to her flat for tea at four o'clock, she says, he will leave with a real goal before dinner.

At four o'clock Ana arrives at Kofi's door with a flask of tea and a bag of paper strips. Kofi clears the kitchen table, sharpens his pencil and feels, for the first time, that something is about to begin.
Kofi writes every dream he has on a paper strip, and the pile reaches nine. Ana looks at them and says that someone who chases nine rabbits usually catches none.
Ana asks Kofi to guess how many hours each goal would need every week. When he adds up the answers, the total is more than a week can hold.
Ana remembers a group of walkers who wanted to climb three peaks in one weekend. They were tired by the second morning, and they did not reach even one summit.
Ana gives him a simple test to try before he decides. He should imagine that it is next January, and ask himself which goal he would be saddest to have ignored.
Kofi pushes the strips aside one at a time and reads each one aloud as it goes. The marathon is the hardest to let go, because he has told people about it for years.
In the end, Kofi circles the word pottery and slides the eight other strips into a kitchen drawer. Ana tells him that they are not gone for ever, because they are only waiting.
Ana says that a goal needs more than a date, because it also needs a reason. Kofi must find out why he wants to make pottery, and he must be honest.
Kofi writes that pottery would be cool and that it might impress his friends. Ana asks him why that matters, and then asks again, until the real answer begins to appear.
Kofi works with numbers all day, and none of them ever leaves the screen. He finds that his real reason is simple: he wants to make something that a person can hold.
Ana says that a good reason is one that would still matter if nobody ever noticed. Kofi writes his on a small card and props it against the old jar on the shelf.

Ana says that a good goal answers three questions. How many will there be, what kind will they be, and who are they for?
After some thought, Kofi chooses to make mugs for his goal. People use mugs every day, a mug is easy to count, and a stranger might actually pay for one.
Kofi writes his goal in one clear sentence at the top of a large sheet. I will sell twenty mugs that I made myself before the thirtieth of June.
Ana tells him that researchers have studied goals for decades. They have found, again and again, that clear and challenging goals tend to bring better results than a vague promise to do your best.
Kofi takes a ruler and draws twenty small boxes in four rows. Each box is one mug, and he will fill it in when a stranger or a friend pays for it.
Kofi tries five mugs, and Ana says it is only a hill that he could climb in his sleep. He tries a hundred, and she says that it is a mountain he cannot climb in six months.
Kofi asks why he should sell the mugs, when he could simply make them. Ana says that a stranger's money is the most honest finish line he could choose.
Kofi counts the weeks from the first of January to the thirtieth of June, and there are about twenty-six. He circles the date on the calendar, and it feels rather like signing a contract.
Kofi copies his goal, his reason and his twenty boxes onto one sheet. He tapes it to the bathroom mirror, where he will see it every morning and every night.

Ana says that from the bottom of a mountain, you often cannot see the top at all. You can only see the next camp, so you walk toward that.

Ana tells Kofi that he should plan backward from the end. He starts at the end of June and asks what must be done just before that, and then before that.
Kofi realises that not every mug he makes will be good. Some will crack and some will turn out wrong, so he decides to make about thirty in order to sell twenty.
Kofi reads that a mug cannot be made in a single evening. It has to dry slowly, be fired in a kiln, be glazed, and then be fired again.
Counting back from the end of June, Kofi sees that he needs time for drying and firing. The last mugs must be made by the middle of May.

He had watched dozens of such videos over the years, and each one had left him warm with longing and then, within the hour, quietly forgotten. Beyond the window the neighbours were already counting down to midnight, and he did not even look up.

On the shelf above the desk sat the evidence of years of wishing: a pottery book whose spine was still stiff, and a lump of clay, bought on an impulse, that had dried into a cracked grey stone. Each spring Kofi dusted them both and put them back exactly where they had been. Neither had ever been used for the purpose that had made him buy it.

On the first morning of the year, Kofi crossed the courtyard of his building and found his neighbour Ana Silva kneeling among her herbs with soil up to her wrists. She was sixty-six, tanned and straight-backed, and she had spent thirty years guiding strangers up mountains before she retired to a first-floor flat and a collection of pots. Without looking up from the mint, she asked him what he wanted from the coming year.

To his own surprise, Kofi found himself confessing that he had wanted to make pottery for years, and that he meant to start someday. Ana pressed the soil firmly around the mint and asked him, quite gently, which day that would be. A wish, she told him, is a lovely thing to own, but it is not yet a goal.

Ana took a pencil from her pocket and drew a cloud on the back of a seed packet, and beside it a small flag planted on a hill. A wish, she explained, drifts and changes shape and can never be reached, whereas a goal is a place with edges, which you can walk toward and stand upon. Afterwards, she said, anyone at all could look at the result and say honestly whether you had arrived.

Ana led him to her kitchen door, where a faded photograph showed a dozen smiling walkers on a ridge, and she told him that in thirty years she had never begun a trip with the word someday. Each expedition, she said, had started with a date, a route and a list on paper, and the dream of the summit had been the smallest part of the preparation. What had carried people to the top, she said, was never the wish itself but the planning behind it.

Wishes stay wishes, Ana said, for three simple reasons: they have no date, they have no first step, and they ask nothing of you today. Because tomorrow always seems a perfectly good moment to begin, a dream can wait politely for decades. The remedy is to give it a deadline and a first step, and to start paying the price before it feels comfortable.

Standing in the courtyard, Kofi counted back over five years of talking, buying and watching, and the sum was uncomfortable. He had spoken about pottery at several dinners, read the first chapter of a book and watched more videos than he could count, yet his hands had never once touched wet clay. It was, he realised, a long and elaborate way of avoiding a single afternoon.

Ana wiped her hands on her trousers and made him an offer that sounded more like an order. If he came to tea at four o'clock and brought a pencil, she said, he would leave her flat before dinner with a real goal in his hand. Kofi, who had spent five years not deciding anything at all, heard himself say yes at once.

Ana arrived at four o'clock exactly, carrying a flask of tea and a bag of paper strips, and Kofi had cleared the kitchen table as if for an examination. He sharpened his pencil twice, although it had been perfectly sharp the first time, and he moved the cups a little to the left. For the first time in years, he felt that something real was about to begin.

Kofi wrote down every goal he had ever half-held, one to a strip of paper, and the pile grew to nine, from pottery and Spanish to a marathon, a garden and piano lessons. Ana looked over his shoulder, counted the strips and observed that someone who chases nine rabbits rarely catches even one. Kofi laughed, then fell silent, when she asked how many of them he had touched in the last year, and he could not honestly answer.

Ana asked him to guess how many hours a week each of the nine goals would honestly need, and Kofi, who earned his living with numbers, wrote the figures down in a neat column. The total was larger than the working week, and it did not leave a single hour for sleeping. Nine goals, he saw, were not a plan but a polite way of arranging for none of them to happen.

Ana remembered a group she once guided, a cheerful party of walkers who had decided to climb three peaks in a single weekend. By the second morning they were exhausted, the weather was turning, and the first summit still lay ahead of them. They walked home that Sunday having reached none, and the guide had learned that ambition is wasted when it is spread too thin.

Ana offered him a test that took only a moment to say and a good deal longer to answer. He was to imagine himself a year from now, sitting in the same chair, and to ask which of these goals he would be saddest to find he had ignored. The strips seemed to change as he looked at them, some of them fading and one growing brighter.
