The marathon was the hardest to surrender, because he had been announcing it at parties for years, but when he asked himself whether he would grieve it in January, the honest answer was no. Only a few strips were left, and one of them was still warm from his hand.

At last Kofi circled the word pottery in thick pencil and slid the other eight strips into the kitchen drawer, where they rested among the batteries and the spare keys. Ana pointed out that nothing had been thrown away, because a dream put in a drawer is only waiting its turn. Kofi found, to his surprise, that the room felt lighter with only one thing left on the table.

Rain began to fall against the window, and Ana poured fresh tea before she spoke again. A goal, she said, needs a reason, and the reason must be strong enough to carry you through the days when the work is dull and nobody is clapping. It was not a question that Kofi had ever asked himself, and he suspected that the answer would not be simple.

Kofi's first answers came quickly and sounded rather weak: pottery looked cool, and it might impress his friends. Ana smiled, and asked him why that mattered, and when he answered she asked again, and then a third time. With each question the answers grew slower and less polished, and they began to sound like something he actually meant.

The third answer, when it finally came, surprised him with its plainness and its quiet certainty. All day long he produced columns of figures that lived on a screen and were forgotten by the end of the month, and what he truly wanted was to make something that another person could hold in their hands. It had nothing whatever to do with being cool, and Kofi felt sure that it would have stayed true even if nobody ever noticed.

Ana told him that a strong reason is one that would still matter if nobody ever praised you, or even noticed. Kofi tested his own against that standard, and it held, so he copied it onto a small white card in his neatest handwriting. He propped it against the old clay jar on the shelf, where he would see it every morning.

Kofi wrote make pottery at the top of a clean sheet and felt rather pleased with himself, until Ana asked how he would know when he had done it. Would one bowl be enough, or a hundred, or a lifetime of Saturdays at the wheel? The sentence, he saw, was another cloud, a little closer to the ground but no less impossible to walk toward.

Ana wrote three small questions in the margin: how many, what kind and for whom. A goal, she said, becomes real the moment it can answer them, because each answer removes a little more fog. Kofi chewed his pencil and discovered that he had never decided any of the three.

After some thought, Kofi chose mugs, and the more he considered them the better they seemed. A mug is useful and honest, it is easy to count, and a stranger might be willing to pay for one, which is the cleanest possible verdict on any piece of work. Better still, a beginner who could make a good mug would have learned most of what the craft had to teach.

Kofi pulled a large sheet toward him and wrote one sentence at the top, pressing hard enough to dent the page underneath: I will sell twenty mugs that I made myself before the thirtieth of June. He read it aloud, and it sounded both more frightening and more exciting than anything he had said in years. Ana nodded slowly, with the quiet approval that she must once have given to walkers who reached a summit.

Ana told him, with the air of someone who enjoyed a good article, that psychologists have studied goal setting for several decades. Over and over, they have found that a specific, challenging target tends to bring better results than a vague intention to do your best, although no rule works perfectly for everyone. A fuzzy aim, it seems, lets us quietly excuse ourselves at every step along the way.

A goal that can be counted can also be checked, so Kofi took a ruler and drew twenty small boxes on a second sheet, in four tidy rows of five. Each box stood for one mug, and he would fill it only when someone had paid for a mug that he had made himself. The empty grid looked a little like a wall waiting for its bricks, and he found that he could hardly wait to begin laying them.

Kofi tried the number five first, and Ana said that it was a hill he could climb in his sleep. He tried a hundred, and she replied that it was a peak he could not reach in six months, however hard he wished. Somewhere between the two lay a goal that would stretch him without breaking him, and twenty, after a long pause, felt like exactly that.

Kofi wondered aloud why he should sell the mugs when he could simply make them and keep them on a shelf. Ana replied that making can always be postponed, whereas selling gives an outside verdict and a finish line that cannot be argued with. A friend might praise a lopsided mug out of kindness, but a stranger with a purse will only pay for what she wants.

A goal without a deadline is only a hope, Ana reminded him, so Kofi turned to June on the wall calendar and circled the thirtieth in thick marker. He counted the weeks from the first of January and found about twenty-six of them, which seemed at once generous and alarmingly few. Drawing the ring, he felt as though he had signed a contract with himself.

That evening Kofi copied his goal, his reason and his twenty boxes onto a single sheet and taped it to the bathroom mirror, at the exact height of his eyes. Ana had advised him to place it where he could not avoid it, because a goal that lives in a drawer behaves like a wish. As he brushed his teeth that night, he read the sentence twice and was pleased to find it still true.

The next morning Ana drew a mountain on the back of an old map, and along the path to its peak she dotted small triangles for tents. Nobody climbs a great mountain in a single push, she explained, because the climb is divided into camps, each of which is a small goal with its own date. A big goal, broken up in the same way, stops being frightening and starts being a route.

Ana added that from the bottom of a mountain you can often see nothing of the summit, because cloud and ridges hide it. A guide never asks her walkers to think about the whole climb at once, but only about the next camp, and then the one after that. Kofi realised that the size of his goal had been frightening him, and that the size of a stage would not.

Kofi sat down with a pad of sticky notes and asked himself what had to happen between now and the end of June. After a little crossing out, four stages remained: learn the basics, practise until the work was dependable, make the mugs, and sell them. They looked sensible and almost easy, written in a row, which Ana warned him was exactly when a plan was most likely to hide its difficulties.

Ana told him to plan backward, which sounded like a riddle until he tried it. Starting at the thirtieth of June on the right-hand end of a long paper timeline, Kofi asked what had to be finished just before that, and then before that, and so on until he reached the left-hand end and today. Slowly the route appeared before him like a path emerging from fog, each step leaning on the one behind it.

As an accountant, Kofi knew that no process runs perfectly, and he suspected that a beginner's clay would waste more than most. Some of his mugs would crack, some would collapse and some would simply be too ugly to sell with a straight face. If twenty were to reach a buyer, he reasoned, he would need to make about thirty and accept the loss without complaint.

A little research taught Kofi that a mug is not made in an evening, however fast the potter's hands might be. The clay has to dry slowly, then be fired in a kiln, then be covered in glaze and fired a second time, and a rushed step can ruin the whole piece. A schedule that ignored all that waiting, he saw, would be a work of fiction.

Counting back from the thirtieth of June, and allowing for the drying, the two firings and the inevitable delays, Kofi found that the last mug would have to leave his hands by the middle of May. It was a new and sobering discovery that the real deadline came six weeks before the one on the calendar. Ana smiled, because every good guide knows that the summit day is decided long before it dawns.

On five index cards, Kofi wrote the milestones that would carry him from the first of January to the market stall, and he laid them in a row on the floor like stepping stones. Each one was a small goal in its own right, with a date, and each could be answered with a plain yes or no. Seeing them side by side, he felt for the first time that the whole distance was something he could cross.

Ana read each card with her glasses low on her nose and said that the milestones must be as checkable as the goal itself. Do some practice, for example, meant nothing, since Kofi could do five minutes and call it a success, so he crossed it out and wrote join a class by the end of January. By the time he had corrected all five, each card could be marked as done or not done.

When the last note was in place, Kofi pinned the timeline along the entire wall of his bedroom, from the first of January in the corner to the market on the far side of the window. Ana stood in the doorway and remarked that a plan is a promise made to your future self, and that promises are easier to keep when they are kept in sight. He lay down that night with the whole journey lined up in front of him like a road.

On the second of January Kofi searched the internet for somewhere to learn, and he was startled to discover a pottery Studio only twenty minutes from his front door. A teacher named Joy Bell ran a beginners' class there on Thursday evenings, lasting ten weeks, and the first lesson was less than two weeks away. Members could also practise on Tuesday evenings and Saturday mornings, which fitted his plan almost too neatly.

For a full minute Kofi's finger hovered over the sign-up button while a familiar voice in his head listed everything that could go wrong. He might look foolish, he might be the worst in the room, and he might discover that he had no talent at all. Then he thought of the card on his shelf, and of Ana's flag, and he pressed the button before the voice could finish.

That week Kofi paid the fee for the class and for the practice hours at the Studio, and the amount made him swallow, since it was larger than he had expected. At home he put a bold tick beside the first milestone on his timeline, join a class by the end of January, and found that a tick was a surprisingly satisfying thing. A goal that had been words on a card for two days was now money spent and a place reserved.

On Thursday evening Kofi pushed open the door of the Studio and stopped on the threshold, overwhelmed by what he saw. Rows of wheels were humming under the bright lights, shelves along the walls were crowded with pale unfinished pots, and everyone he could see wore a smear of clay as casually as a watch. The air smelled of wet earth after rain, and he felt at once like an intruder and like someone arriving home.

Joy Bell, the teacher, was a cheerful woman with grey streaks in her hair and clay drying on her forearms, and she welcomed the eight new students as though they were old friends. Everybody in this room, she announced, had once started with a single lump of clay and no idea what to do with it. Kofi found himself placed between Tomas, a retired baker with enormous gentle hands, and Lena, an art student who laughed easily.

The first lesson, Joy announced, was wedging, a kind of kneading that pushes the air out of the clay and makes it even in texture. Kofi leaned his weight into the cold lump and rolled it forward and back, feeling the strain gather in his shoulders after only a few minutes. To his surprise he was smiling, because after years of watching he was finally doing it.

At last Kofi sat at a wheel and set it spinning, and within seconds his lump of clay slid sideways and flew off onto the floor with a smack. He braced himself for mockery, but the laughter that rose from the class was warm and sympathetic, because every one of them had suffered the same indignity. Joy retrieved the clay, patted it back into a ball and said that centring is the hardest part of all, and the part everyone must do.

At eight o'clock Kofi washed his hands at the big stained sink and found clay lodged deep beneath his fingernails, where it would remain for days. He had made nothing worth keeping, only a lopsided pinch pot that Joy had insisted was a good start, and yet he rode the bus home smiling at his reflection in the window. After five years of wishing, a single evening of doing had changed the colour of the day.

Ana's advice at their next tea was that Kofi should always be able to name his very next action, however small, because a goal without one is another cloud. He wrote a line on a yellow sticky note and pressed it to the lid of his laptop, where it would greet him every evening: book the Tuesday and Saturday sessions. The next step, once it had a name, took less than three minutes to complete, and it felt like a door opening.

Ana introduced him to a small trick, the if-then plan, in which you decide ahead of time exactly when and where you will act. Kofi wrote that if it was Tuesday at six o'clock, then he would leave the office and walk straight to the Studio, and he set a phone alarm and hung his apron by the front door as reminders. Research on such plans suggests that they have helped many people follow through, because the decision is already made when the moment arrives.

Ana pointed to a photograph on her wall in which black clouds were piling up behind a jagged ridge. A good guide, she said, plans for fog and storms as carefully as she plans for sunshine, because the mountain does not care about anyone's schedule. She suggested that Kofi's plan, so far, was a plan for a sunny day.

Ana told him about a young guide she had once trained, a cheerful optimist who pictured every trip in bright sunshine and packed accordingly. He forgot the rain jackets on the one day it mattered, and his group came down the mountain cold, wet and silent. Optimism, Ana said, is a fine companion, but it should never be allowed to carry the bags.

Some research, Ana said, suggests that people who picture their success together with the obstacles in its way may prepare better than those who picture only the happy ending. The findings are not perfect or universal, but the idea seemed to Kofi both sensible and slightly alarming. Dreaming of success alone, it seemed, can make the mind relax too early, as if the work had already been done.

Kofi fetched a fresh sheet and wrote Obstacles at the top, and then he made himself list everything that could realistically stop him. Tiredness after long days at the office came first, followed by the cost of clay and firing, and finally, in smaller letters, the fear of looking foolish. Ana told him to leave a space beside each, because every obstacle deserves an answer written in advance.

For the first obstacle, tiredness, Kofi wrote a rule beside it: if I feel too tired after work, then I will eat a snack and go to the Studio anyway, for half an hour only. He knew from experience that the sofa had a persuasive voice at six o'clock and that a promise of thirty minutes was much easier to keep than a promise of two hours. Most evenings, he suspected, the half hour would quietly stretch into something much longer once he was there.

Beside the fear of looking foolish, Kofi wrote the memory of the first evening: if I feel foolish, then I will remember that everyone in this room once sent a lump of clay flying. He thought of Tomas laughing as his own first attempt collapsed, and of Lena holding up a grey, misshapen bowl as if it were a trophy. Fear, he began to see, is much weaker when it has been named and answered in writing.

With three coloured highlighters, Kofi went through a typical week and marked the hours that already belonged to something else, and then the hours that were truly free. Five of them, he found, could be given to the goal each week, spread across Tuesday evening, Thursday evening and Saturday morning. It was not a great deal of time, but spread across twenty-six weeks it would add up to more than a hundred hours.

Since he was an accountant, Kofi treated the cost of the goal like a small project budget, with lines for clay, glaze, firing fees, packing materials and a market stall. The total was manageable, but only if he began setting money aside straight away, so he labelled a jar Clay and promised it a small deposit every payday. There was an odd pleasure in discovering that a dream could be priced and then paid for in instalments.

Kofi knew that March would be the dangerous month, because the firm's year-end accounts were due and the office filled with panicked clients and late evenings. He explained his plan to his colleague Priya, who raised an eyebrow and then promised to cover for him on Tuesdays, and he entered his pottery hours in the work calendar as if they were meetings with an important client. An appointment written down, he had learned, is much harder to cancel than a good intention.

Kofi taped the finished sheet of obstacles inside the kitchen cupboard door, where he would see it every time he reached for a mug. Ana warned him that no list could foresee every storm, and that when an unexpected one arrived he must be willing to change the route but never the destination. It was the first time he had thought of a plan as something that could bend without breaking.

By the end of January, Kofi could centre a lump of clay on the wheel more often than not, and he felt rather proud of the achievement. The walls of his cylinders, however, remained a disaster, leaning and wobbling and finally folding in on themselves with a soft sigh like a tired animal lying down. Each collapse brought him to the same uncomfortable conclusion: that the hardest part of the craft was exactly the part he had been avoiding.

Joy had watched hundreds of beginners come and go, and she told Kofi that most of them repeated the easy part of the craft because it felt pleasant and made them look competent. Real progress, she said, comes from practising the hardest part, the stubborn piece that keeps going wrong, and from doing it with attention rather than merely with repetition. It was uncomfortable advice, because it meant welcoming failure in the open instead of dodging it for months.

That Saturday Kofi decided to practise nothing but the walls, and he made twenty cylinders in a single morning, cutting each one in half with a wire to check the thickness. Each time he altered one small thing, whether the speed of the wheel, the angle of his fingers or the amount of water, and noticed what happened. By the fifteenth cylinder he could feel the clay rising evenly beneath his hands, and the sensation was unlike anything he had known.

On a bitterly cold Tuesday the rain fell all day, and by six o'clock Kofi was tired after a long and pointless meeting, and the sofa was whispering his name. He remembered the rule taped inside the cupboard door, ate a banana, pulled on his coat and cycled through the puddles to the Studio for half an hour only. He stayed for ninety minutes, and on the ride home the rain no longer seemed to matter.

Joy took one of Kofi's best mugs, which he had been rather proud of, and sliced it in half from top to bottom with a wire. The base was as thick as a biscuit, she pointed out, which would trap the heat and probably crack the mug in the kiln, and nothing on the outside gave any hint of it. Honest feedback, Kofi realised, is a window onto exactly the faults that you cannot see for yourself.

Encouraged, Kofi asked Tomas to look at his work as well, and the old baker turned each mug over, tapped it and offered several blunt observations. It stung more than he expected, because it is one thing to hear kind encouragement and another to hear exactly where the work falls short. Ana, when he told her, said that honest feedback is a mirror, and that only a fool avoids mirrors.

Beside the tally of mugs, Kofi taped a second chart to the bathroom mirror, a grid of small circles with one for every session he planned to attend. Each time he returned from the Studio he coloured in a dot with a green pen, and he discovered that this tiny ritual gave the evening a sense of completion. The rows of green grew steadily, and he began to look forward to filling them.

After five weeks of Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays, the grid showed fourteen coloured dots with only one gap, and Kofi studied it with real satisfaction. On days when his mugs looked no better than the week before, the chart still offered a small, solid proof that he was doing what he had promised to do. Progress in the clay was slow and uneven, but progress in the effort was visible at a glance.

Ana pointed out that Kofi could not control how many people would want a mug in June, but he could control how often he sat at the wheel. She suggested that he add goals for his actions to his goal for the result, such as three sessions every week, because actions are the part of the future that belong to us. Kofi wrote the new line beneath the old one and felt, to his surprise, a good deal calmer than before.

At the end of February Joy lifted the lid of the kiln, and there, among the shelves of pale pots, stood Kofi's first finished mug, glazed a deep and uneven blue. It leaned a little to the left, the handle was too small for a normal finger and the lip was not quite level, but it held water, and it was entirely his own. He drew a bold tick beside the milestone on his wall and drank a cup of tea from it that same evening.

By the second week of March the excitement of the first weeks had drained away like water from a basin. It was raining, the apron lay folded on the chair where he had left it, and Kofi could not summon a single persuasive reason for leaving the warm flat. The goal that had seemed so bright in January now looked like a very long list of chores.

When Kofi confessed the problem, Ana was not in the least surprised, and she poured him another cup of tea. On every long expedition, she said, the fourth day was the worst, when the thrill of the start was long forgotten and the summit was nowhere in sight. Walkers who understood that the middle is always heavy simply kept walking, and did not take their weariness as a sign that the plan had failed.

Kofi counted the weeks on the wall calendar with the tip of his pencil: ten behind him and sixteen still ahead. The arithmetic ought to have been comforting, but it was the numbers on the shelf that troubled him, because his mugs were still thick, crooked and unconvincing. He could not shake the thought that he had spent a quarter of his time and had very little to show for it.

Ana's remedy for such days was almost embarrassingly small: shrink the step until it is too easy to refuse. Instead of promising himself an evening at the wheel, Kofi was to set a timer for ten minutes and allow himself to stop when it rang. The difficulty of a task, she said, usually lies in beginning it, and ten minutes is a very short wall to climb.

That evening Kofi dragged himself to the Studio, set the timer for ten minutes and sat down at the wheel with a sigh. When the alarm rang, he was so absorbed in a half-pulled cylinder that he silenced it without looking, and he worked on until the caretaker began switching off the lights. Starting, he reflected on the long ride home, had been the only truly difficult part of the evening.

As expected, the firm's busy season descended in the third week of March, and Kofi found himself buried beneath year-end accounts and demanding clients. He missed a Tuesday session, then a Thursday, and the two gaps in his dot chart looked like missing teeth in a smile. For the first time since January, the plan on his wall felt like a reproach rather than a promise.

Then, exhausted and overworked, Kofi caught a bad flu and spent a whole week in bed under a heap of blankets with a fever and a hammering head. Six days passed without a minute of practice, and the row of empty circles on the bathroom mirror seemed to grow longer each time he shuffled in to look at it. He lay awake in the small hours of the night wondering whether the whole project had quietly died.

When Ana arrived with a pot of soup, Kofi was tempted to announce that the project was over, and he said as much in a hoarse voice. She listened without argument, ladled out a bowlful and told him that missing one session is an accident but that missing two in a row is the beginning of a habit. The goal had not failed, she said, because a goal is only abandoned when you stop returning to it.

The following Tuesday Kofi walked into the Studio with a scarf around his neck, still weak and faintly ashamed, and he half expected a reprimand. Joy simply smiled, said that she was glad to see him and handed him a lump of clay to wedge, which was all that his arms could manage for the first five minutes. Nobody in the busy room had been counting his absence except himself, and the discovery was a great relief.

At home that night Kofi coloured in a single green dot, and then he stood there for a while considering the gap beside it. He could have filled it in with a lie, or torn the page off the mirror and started a fresh one, but instead he left the blank row exactly as it was. The chart, he decided, was meant to tell the truth, and the truth included a week of fever and a Tuesday when he went back.

In the days after the flu, Kofi worked up the courage to ask Ana for a favour. Would she meet him once a month, he wondered, simply to hear how the goal was going? He had noticed that his promises to himself bent more easily than his promises to other people, and that the thought of a conversation on a fixed date made the work in between feel more serious.

Ana agreed, but on conditions, which she wrote out in the margin of the calendar in her upright guide's handwriting. Kofi was to bring his numbers without decoration, he was to bring one real problem rather than a list of complaints, and he was to leave every meeting with a single decision made. A check-in that produced only sympathy, she added, was a pleasant chat and not much else.

At their first meeting, Kofi laid his tally chart and his dot chart on the table, along with an honest account of the missed week. Ana studied them with her pencil tapping softly against her teeth, and then she asked the question that would become the heart of every check-in: what will you do differently next month? He had to think for a long time before he found an answer he believed.

Over dinner on a Friday, Kofi finally told his friend Dan about the twenty mugs, the date and the Studio. Ana had warned him that the research on announcing goals to other people is mixed, since some studies suggest that it helps and others that it can make us feel as though we have already achieved something. Kofi decided that he would tell people for the pleasure of being asked how it was going.

Dan laughed and teased him for about a minute, and then, to Kofi's surprise, he put down his fork and said that he wanted to buy the very first mug. Kofi realised that the best people to tell were not those who would simply applaud, but those who would ask, a month later, how things were going. A goal that other people expect you to report on is rather harder to forget.

At the office the following week, Kofi hesitated and then showed Priya a photograph of his first blue mug, lopsided handle and all. She studied it with the critical eye of a woman who had bought many gifts, and then told him that it was lovely and that he should put her name down for one. It was a small remark, but it made the mug feel, for the first time, like a product rather than an accident.

Remembering Ana's advice that the first step should be as easy as possible, Kofi cleared a corner of the flat and set up a small table by the window. A bucket of clay sat beneath a damp cloth, a sketchbook lay open beside it, and a roll of tools waited in the corner like a patient assistant. Any small task could now be started in less than a minute, with no preparation at all.

Kofi discovered that the surroundings could do much of the work that willpower would otherwise have to do. When he practised at home he put his phone in a drawer beyond the reach of casual temptation, and he left the sketchbook open on the table with a pencil on top. The right choice became the easy one, and the wrong choice cost him a small and irritating effort.

One night a bright advertisement for a Spanish course appeared on Kofi's screen, and for ten minutes he was seriously tempted to sign up at once. He thought of the drawer in the kitchen and the eight strips inside it, and he understood that a new idea can feel more exciting than an old goal precisely because it has not yet become difficult. He closed the laptop with a firm click and decided that the idea could wait politely until the beginning of July.

Kofi opened his notebook to a clean page and wrote After June across the top in capital letters. He copied down the Spanish course and two other ideas that had been nagging at him, and he felt a surprising wave of relief, as though he had put down a heavy bag. An idea that is written down and given a date, he found, stops pulling at your sleeve.

Ana suggested that a goal needs a weekly pulse, and so on Sunday evenings Kofi began to sit down with his notebook for ten quiet minutes. He asked himself three questions and answered each in a line or two: what went well this week, what got in the way, and what were the next three steps. It was a small habit, hardly more than a cup of tea with a pencil, yet it turned each week into a lesson.

In his first review Kofi wrote, beneath the heading What went well, that he had pulled up the walls of three mugs in a row without a single collapse. It seemed a modest thing to record, but seeing it in ink made it feel solid, a fact that bad days could not take away. He realised that he had been so busy noticing his failures that he had never paid his successes the same attention.

Under the second heading, Kofi wrote what had got in the way, and he found it much easier to be honest on paper than in his head. On Tuesday he had stayed late at the office, reached the Studio tired and hungry and produced three poor mugs in two hours, none of them worth keeping. Naming the problem plainly, without excuses or blame, was oddly relieving, like turning on a light in a cluttered room.

The final heading in the review was the one that mattered most, because it turned the lessons into action. Kofi listed three steps for the week ahead, each small enough to be finished and clear enough to be checked: throw six cylinders on Saturday, trim the two dry mugs and send an email about the market. When Monday morning arrived, he did not have to wonder for a single moment what he ought to do.

Kofi wanted a second colour to go with his blue, and Joy recommended a deep green. She advised him to test it on small clay tiles before risking a whole mug, so that any mistake would cost him a scrap of clay and not an evening's work. It was a lesson in running small experiments to learn quickly, and the row of numbered tiles looked like a miniature gallery.

After the firing, Kofi lined up the tiles on the windowsill and chose the blue and the green, which looked like deep water and wet leaves in the afternoon light. Joy remarked that these were friendly, forgiving colours that suited almost any kitchen, and that a beginner who could rely on two glazes would waste far less time than one who tried twelve. Fewer choices, Kofi found, made the work easier and the evenings calmer, and he stopped agonising over colours.

After several weeks of Sunday notes, a pattern began to show itself in Kofi's handwriting: his Tuesday sessions were always the weakest. He had been going home first, sinking into a chair and then dragging himself out again, and the delay was killing his energy, so he began to pack a sandwich and walk straight from the office to the Studio. The following Tuesday turned out to be the best session of the whole month, and he wrote that in his notebook.

One Sunday Kofi read all his reviews in order, from the first awkward line to the most recent, and the effect was startling. Day by day he had been unable to see any change, yet the pages showed collapsing walls turning into steady ones, cracked bases into sound ones and shaky resolve into a routine. Progress, he realised, is nearly invisible from the inside and unmistakable from a distance.

The reviews also revealed that his handles were the weakest part of every mug, too small, too thin and often detached by the time the clay dried. Remembering Joy's advice about practising the hardest part, Kofi spent two whole sessions pulling nothing but handles, thirty of them in all, until his fingers could feel the right thickness without thinking. The reward came at the next review, where the line what went well was suddenly a long one.

Ana tapped the calendar and observed that the halfway camp was only a few days away, which meant that it was time for a proper look at the whole plan. Kofi had spent thirteen weeks learning how to work, and the next thirteen would show what the work was worth. She suggested that they meet on the bench by the river on the first of April, and she asked him to bring everything.

On the first of April, thirteen weeks after the circle on the calendar, Kofi and Ana sat on a bench by the river beneath trees thick with pink blossom. He had brought every chart, every notebook and the folded timeline from his bedroom wall, and he spread them across their knees as the wind tried to carry them away. Halfway, Ana said, is the best place to stop and look at the whole mountain.

Ana asked him a question that was simple to put and surprisingly hard to answer. If he were choosing a goal today, knowing everything that he had learned in thirteen weeks, would he choose the same one? Kofi watched the river slide past for a long while before he said yes, and that one word told him more about the reason on his card than the card itself.

Then they turned to the numbers on the page, which were considerably less kind than the blossom. Kofi had seven finished mugs on his shelf, whereas the timeline pinned to his wall had said that by the first of April he should have ten, and not one box on the tally chart had been filled. His stomach tightened, since the gap was small but undeniable, and he was behind.

Kofi's first instinct was to retreat, to move the deadline to July or to quietly lower the number to fifteen. Ana shook her head, and said that when a plan falls behind, you ask what can change in the plan before you ask whether the goal must change. A goal that moves whenever it becomes difficult, she added, is not a goal but a mood.

Ana took an envelope from her pocket and wrote four words on the back: hours, method, speed, order. These were the things that Kofi was free to change, she explained, while the goal and the date remained where they were. He studied the list and understood that for three months he had been treating the whole plan as a single block, when it was really a machine with several adjustable parts.

At the next class Kofi described his problem, and Joy showed him how experienced potters work in batches. Instead of finishing one mug at a time, he was to throw six in a row, then trim all six, then attach six handles, so that each movement was repeated while his hands still remembered it. The saving in time was startling, and, to his delight, the mugs began to look like members of one family.

As an accountant, Kofi found the arithmetic strangely soothing, since a problem with numbers in it was a problem he could solve. He needed about thirty mugs thrown by the middle of May, he had seven, and six weeks remained, so the plan required twenty-three more at a pace of nearly four a week. Four mugs in a week, with a batch of six on the wheel, seemed a challenge but not an impossibility.

Kofi turned the figure into a weekly target that he could actually act upon: six mugs thrown every week, in the hope of keeping at least four. The extra two were a cushion against the mugs that would collapse or crack, and he felt a good deal better knowing that his plan allowed for failure from the start. He wrote the target on a new card in large letters and propped it beside the card that held his reason.

That evening Kofi took down the old timeline and drew a new one on the bedroom wall, with fresh dates for each batch of mugs. Several tasks had moved and one had been struck out altogether, but the finish line stood in the same place on the thirtieth of June, and the revision felt like a repair and not a defeat. He pinned the last note in place and stepped back, and for the first time in a fortnight he felt pleased with himself.

Before they parted, Ana reminded him of the third rule of their meetings, that he must leave with one decision made. His was simple and firm, to work in batches of six from the following Tuesday, and he walked home through the park with blossom drifting down around him like slow snow. He had been behind and uncertain an hour earlier, and now he felt behind but sure of the road.

After a long wait, Kofi opened the kiln on his first full batch of eight mugs, and for a moment he stood quite still. Four of them were perfect, glowing blue and green in the light from the door, but the other four were split by long, ugly cracks that ran from the base to the rim. The hours of work that lay inside those four mugs seemed to drain out of the room.

Joy was not surprised, and she took the cracked mug from his hands as gently as if it had been a wounded bird. Pots crack for many reasons, she said, among them uneven thickness, trapped water, drying too fast and heat that rises too quickly, and every potter she had ever known had opened a kiln to a disaster of some kind. The real question, she told him, was never whether it would happen again, but what you chose to do afterwards.

Kofi sat on a stool among the shelves and counted the loss with the cold arithmetic of his profession: four mugs, about twelve hours of work and a precious week of drying and firing. He was behind again, with barely eleven weeks left, and a small, unpleasant voice began to suggest that he had never been good enough for this. He let it speak for a minute, and then he asked Joy to help him find the cause.

Joy laid the four ruined mugs side by side on the table, and the two of them examined the cracks like detectives bent over a crime scene. Nearly all of them began at the base and climbed the walls in a thin, jagged line, and Kofi remembered with a wince what Joy had said weeks ago about the thickness of his bottoms. He had improved, she observed, but not quite enough, and he had also dried the batch on a shelf above the radiator.

Back at home, Kofi wrote a short plan for the next batch: he would trim the bottoms until they were no thicker than the walls, and dry the mugs slowly under plastic sheeting, far from the radiator. Joy had advised changing only one or two things at a time, because changing everything at once teaches nothing. By the sixth mug of the next batch he could feel the right thickness through the clay without measuring.

A week later Kofi lifted the lid of the kiln with his heart in his throat, and this time the news was good. Seven of the eight mugs were sound and gleaming, with only one crack, a hairline one near the handle, and the changes he had made had plainly worked. He understood that the earlier failure had been worth more than a dozen easy successes, because it had told him exactly what to fix.

At the monthly check-in Ana looked at the broken mugs and the whole ones lined up on her table, and she did not offer sympathy. A failure, she said, is information that the world has been kind enough to deliver, and a good guide, when a route is blocked, never blames the mountain but asks what the mountain has just taught her. Kofi's decision for the month, which he said aloud, was to write every lesson down.

Kofi pinned a new sheet to the wall, headed Lessons, and began to fill it in his smallest handwriting. Thin bottoms, slow drying, test the glaze on tiles and change one thing at a time were the first four lines, and he resolved to add another each time something went wrong. A mistake written down, he found, had a way of turning from a wound into a tool.

Then came a bad Thursday on which absolutely nothing worked, and the evening seemed to go wrong from its very first minute. Three mugs in a row collapsed on the wheel, a handle came away in his hand, and Joy was busy with another student, so there was nobody to tell him that it would be all right. He walked home in the dark with clay in his hair and lay awake for hours, seriously considering whether twenty mugs mattered at all.

In the grey light of the morning Kofi took down the little white card and read the sentence he had written in January about making something that another person could hold. It was exactly as true as it had been on the first day, and it did not depend on his mood, on the weather or on a single bad Thursday. He put the card back, picked up his apron and went to the Studio to begin again.

At the end of April Kofi lined up every finished mug on the windowsill, eighteen of them, and judged each against a list he had written himself: even walls, a level rim, a firm handle and a glaze without flaws. Ten passed, and the other eight went onto a lower shelf as seconds for his own kitchen. It was the milestone that he had pinned on the wall in January, and he had reached it nearly on time.

With a green pen Kofi ticked the third milestone on his timeline and showed it to Ana, who looked at the ten mugs with real pleasure. She told him that a goal which celebrates only the finish line leaves long stretches of the journey without a reward, and that effort deserves a small celebration along the way. Praise for the work itself, she said, keeps the work alive long after the first excitement has gone.

To celebrate, Kofi took Dan to a small restaurant on the corner, the kind with candles in bottles and a menu written on a blackboard. It was a modest reward for ten good mugs, but eating together made the achievement feel real in a way that a tick on a chart never could. Dan raised a glass, and the two of them toasted a handful of lopsided blue cups.

Kofi had brought one of the blue mugs in his bag, and Dan turned it in the candlelight, running his thumb over the glaze and weighing it in his palm. Then he asked, quite casually, how much Kofi was going to charge, and Kofi realised with a jolt that he had planned for everything except the price. A goal about selling, he thought wryly, had been missing the one number that decides whether anyone will buy.

That night, unable to sleep, Kofi scrolled through pottery pictures on his phone until he came upon a shelf of flawless mugs made by a professional with ten thousand followers. Every rim was perfect, every glaze a flawless sheet of colour, and beside them his own ten mugs seemed suddenly clumsy and childish. The warm glow of the evening drained from him as he lay in the dark.

When Kofi described the pictures at their next meeting, Ana nodded as if she had met the problem before on many a mountain. Comparing yourself with an expert, she said, is like comparing your first week of climbing with a guide of thirty years, and the only fair comparison is with the person you were yesterday. The expert's shelf, she added, held a decade of work, and Kofi's held four months.

At home Kofi found the photograph of his very first mug from February and propped it beside one of his latest, and the difference made him laugh out loud. The first was thick, crooked and glazed in a lumpy blue, whereas the new one had thin, even walls, a level rim and a handle that curved as gracefully as a question mark. Four months had changed his hands, even if the changes had been invisible day by day.

Kofi sat at the kitchen table with a calculator and a heap of receipts and treated the question as he would have treated a client's accounts. Clay, glaze, kiln fees, the Studio's membership and the packing materials all went into a column, divided by the number of mugs that he expected to finish. The result was a good deal higher than he had guessed, and it did not yet include a single hour of his own time.

Joy told him sternly that beginners always forget to count their own time, which is why so many of them work for nothing. She took him to a craft shop in the old town, where handmade mugs stood on a long wooden shelf with their prices written on small brown tags. Some were more expensive than he had expected, and a few were cheaper than the cost he had calculated.

After careful thought Kofi settled on eighteen pounds a mug, a figure that covered his costs, gave a little back for his time and seemed fair to anyone who might hold one in a shop. He wrote it on a small card and pinned it by the tally chart, and he felt a curious mixture of pride and terror at having put a price on something he had made. It meant that twenty mugs would bring him a little over three hundred and fifty pounds.

In the first week of May, Dan counted eighteen pounds into Kofi's palm, picked up a blue mug and held it against his chest as though it might be taken away. Kofi stood for a moment with the notes in his hand, and then he went home and filled in the first of the twenty boxes with a thick black pen. It was only a very small square on a sheet of paper, and yet it felt enormous.

That evening Kofi sat by the open window and looked at the money for a long time, turning it over like something rare. It was only eighteen pounds, and Dan was a friend, who would have been kind about a leaning tower of mud, but somebody had still paid for a thing that Kofi had made. Dan's message that night said that he would have paid double, and Kofi read it three times.

Ana studied the filled box with pleasure, but she did not let him stop there. A friend, she reminded him, is a gentle customer who buys partly out of affection, and the real test of a mug is whether a stranger who owes you nothing will part with money for it. The market would supply that test, but there were weeks to go, and she thought he should practise selling before then.

At the office, Priya bought two mugs, one for herself and one as a birthday present for her mother, and she paid in cash and with a flourish. She unwrapped them in front of the whole department, and within the hour three colleagues had asked Kofi when they could see more. Kofi, who had once been afraid to admit that he made pottery at all, now fielded questions across the desks with a shy grin.

Kofi's older sister Abena, a nurse who worked long and unpredictable shifts, spotted one of the new green mugs in the background of a video call and demanded to know where it had come from. When he confessed that he had made it, she shrieked with such joy that their mother could be heard asking from the next room what had happened. She paid the following Sunday and sent a photograph of it steaming on her kitchen table.

At the Studio the following Thursday, Tomas picked up one of Kofi's green mugs from the shelf and turned it over in his large baker's hands, checking the base the way a man checks a loaf. He paid for it on the spot, and said gruffly that it would hold his morning tea and that he expected the handle to last. Coming from a man who had judged so many of Kofi's failures, the approval felt like a medal.

By the middle of May Kofi had sold five mugs, one to Dan, two to Priya, one to Abena and one to Tomas, and he filled in five boxes on the tally chart with a steady hand. Fifteen remained, which was a larger number than he liked, and every one of the five buyers was a friend or a colleague. If the goal were to be reached, strangers would have to buy the rest.

Kofi had put the task off for weeks, so on a Sunday evening he made it the first of his three steps and wrote to Rosa Quinn, who ran Riverside Market in the old square. He asked whether a table was free on the last Saturday of June, what it cost and what he needed to bring. His thumb hovered over the button, and then, because the next action was only to press it, he did.

Rosa Quinn replied the next morning, warm and brief: a table was free on the last Saturday of June, and she would keep it for him if he paid a small deposit by the end of the week. Kofi paid that same evening, and the amount was trivial, but the moment the money left his account the finish line stopped being a circle on a calendar and became a place with a name and a time. He could feel the date coming toward him like a train, steady and impossible to stop.

On his timeline Kofi wrote stall booked in firm capitals and stepped back to look at it, feeling at once terrified and delighted. When he told Ana, she said that a fixed public date was like a camp on the mountain from which there is no sensible way back, and that this was precisely its value. The goal had become something that other people were now expecting him to do.

In the middle of May, Kofi looked at the red note on his calendar and understood that the deadline behind the deadline had almost arrived. Two weeks remained before the last day on which a mug could be thrown, dried, fired, glazed and fired again in time for the market, and he wanted to know precisely where he stood. A guide, Ana had once said, counts her food before the storm and not during it.

Kofi counted the mugs shelf by shelf, writing each number in chalk on a small slate. Fourteen good mugs were finished and five of them were already sold, eleven more were drying or waiting for the kiln, and the total came to twenty-five, a little more than the twenty he had needed. The extra five were the cushion that he had built into the plan in January, and it was already being eaten.

On the last Saturday for throwing, Kofi sat at the wheel for three hours without once looking at the clock, and the batch of six that he made was the best of his life. His hands knew the weight of the clay, the speed of the wheel and the pressure of the walls, and the lessons of four months moved through them without any thought. Joy watched from a stool and said nothing, which, from her, was high praise.

Glaze day required a different kind of concentration, quieter and more fearful than the wheel. Kofi dipped each mug into the bucket of blue or green with a slow turn of the wrist, then wiped the base clean with a damp sponge, knowing that one careless drip could weld a mug to the kiln shelf. By the end of the afternoon his shoulders ached, and eleven mugs stood on the boards, wet and shining.

Joy switched on the kiln, and then there was nothing to do but wait, for the heat had to climb slowly and the kiln had to cool even more slowly. Ana remarked that patience is a part of every good plan, since some steps cannot be rushed however badly you want them to be, and the wise guide builds the waiting into the schedule. Kofi paced about the flat for two long evenings and rearranged the same shelf three times, like a man waiting for news.

When Kofi finally opened the kiln, the shelves held a small, bright miracle: most of the mugs shone blue and green, perfect and sound. Three of them, however, were pale and patchy, because the glaze had gone on too thinly, and the only remedy was to coat them again and fire them a second time. It cost a week, and it was the kind of delay that his four spare days could absorb.

At the check-in at the end of the month, Kofi and Ana went through the milestones one at a time with the pencil of a careful auditor. Every one of them had been met, apart from the last firing, which was three days late, and Ana said that on a mountain, three days behind would have been considered a triumph. The spare days that he had built into the plan in January had done their quiet work, and nobody but the two of them would ever know.

Late in May, after the long weeks of the busy season, Kofi was so tired that he sat on the edge of his bed holding the apron, almost certain that he would not go. Then he remembered Ana's old remedy, set a timer for ten minutes and went to the Studio, telling himself that he might leave when it rang. He stayed for two hours, glazing the three pale mugs for the second time, and he never even heard the timer ring.

After the Thursday session the old class gathered around the Studio table with tea and biscuits, and Tomas and Lena promised solemnly to come to Kofi's stall on the day. Joy handed him a long list of tips scribbled on the back of a delivery slip, among them to wrap each mug separately, to pack small boxes tightly and to carry a spare roll of tape. He tucked the paper into his notebook as carefully as if it were a map of unknown country.

At the end of May, Kofi stood in front of the shelf in the evening light and counted twenty good mugs ready for the market, with five more already living in other people's kitchens. They stood in rows of blue and green, a little different from one another, and there was nothing in the whole line of which he was ashamed. A great many hours had gone into making them, and every one of those hours was somehow visible.

In the last week of June, Kofi wrapped each mug separately in newspaper, as Joy had instructed, and laid them in boxes with scrunched paper packed tightly between them. A long checklist lay beside the boxes, and he ticked each task off in pencil with the care of a man who knew how easily the smallest thing is forgotten on the morning of an important day. Planning, he reflected, is largely the art of remembering things in advance, while there is still time to act.

The checklist ran to thirty items, from the obvious ones like the tablecloth and the paper bags to the ones a beginner would never think of until it was too late. There was a bag of coins for giving change, a roll of tape, two pens, a bottle of water, sunscreen and a folding stool, and an old shoebox to hold the takings. Joy's rule, which he copied in capitals, was that a stall without change is a stall without customers.

Abena arrived that evening with a bag of paints and a mischievous grin, and the two of them sat on the kitchen floor to make signs for the stall. One showed the price in clear black numbers, and the other, in curling green letters, announced that every mug was made by hand by Kofi in this very town. Hearing her read it out loud, he realised that he had never before described himself as a maker.

Kofi was shy about talking to strangers, and Ana, who had spent thirty years managing nervous walkers, recognised the problem at once. She turned herself into a series of customers, an impatient one, a curious one and one who wanted a discount, and made him practise a greeting, an answer to every question and the price without looking at his feet. By the fifth customer, a stern woman with a very large handbag, he was almost enjoying himself.

On a small card he wrote three if-then rules for the market, and he read them aloud twice. If someone picks up a mug, then he would say hello and let them hold it in peace, and if a customer asked how it was made, then he would tell the story of his first lump of clay. If nobody came for an hour, he would stay in his chair and keep smiling, because the plan could not work if the plan-maker walked away.

Kofi had prepared for tiredness, fear and cracked mugs, but he had never planned for rain at an open-air market. Ana fetched a faded green tarp from her mountain days, which had sheltered many a wet camp, and showed him how to rig it above a stall with four ropes and two poles. A good guide, she said, always carries a roof, even on a day when she does not expect to use it.

On Friday morning Kofi checked the forecast, and it promised showers in the afternoon, with the cheerful vagueness of weather forecasts everywhere. A year ago, he realised, such a prediction would have made him cancel the whole project, but now he only smiled and checked the ropes of the tarp. He could not control the sky, but he could control his readiness for it.

On Friday night Kofi lay awake with his thoughts running ahead of him like children, picturing empty tables, rude customers and mugs breaking in the boxes. At last he got up, took the little white card from the shelf and read the sentence he had written in January about making something another person could hold. The nervousness did not vanish, but it settled, as dust settles when a window is closed.

Ana appeared at his door on Friday evening with a flask of tea and no particular agenda, and she sat at the table and said very little for a quarter of an hour. Then she remarked that on a mountain the summit day is mostly decided by the weeks of preparation that precede it, and that he had done the work and could now simply walk. Whatever the market brought on the morrow, she added, nobody could ever take away the six months of work behind him.

At six o'clock on Saturday morning Dan arrived with his battered car, yawning and holding two paper cups of coffee, and the two of them loaded the boxes, the signs, the tarp and the folding table into the back. Kofi counted everything twice against the list and found nothing missing, which in itself felt like a small victory. The street was empty and gold, and the day ahead stretched out like a road.

By seven o'clock on the last Saturday of June, Kofi had set up his table in a corner of the old square, with the cloth smoothed, the signs propped up and the mugs in neat rows of blue and green. In his pocket was a small card with twenty boxes drawn on it, copied from the sheet on his mirror at home. Around him the other stallholders were unpacking jam, flowers and bread, and the morning air smelled of coffee.

For the whole of the first hour, absolutely nobody stopped at Kofi's stall, and the empty path in front of him seemed to grow wider. People strolled past with coffee and shopping bags, glancing at the mugs and moving on, and every instinct he had urged him to hide behind the boxes or to pack up and go home. He remembered the rule on his card, stayed in his chair and kept smiling at every passer-by, which, as it happened, was exactly what the plan required.

At last a woman in a yellow coat stopped, picked up a green mug and turned it over in her hands, and Kofi, remembering his card, said hello and then said nothing at all. She weighed the mug, ran her thumb around its smooth rim and asked whether he had made it himself, and when he said yes she smiled, took out her purse and paid eighteen pounds. He filled in the first market box on his card with a hand that shook slightly, and he did not mind that she saw.

As the morning went on, customers told him what they liked, and Kofi, who would never have asked directly, listened with growing fascination. The green mugs were by far the most popular, a handle that fitted the whole hand mattered more than he had thought, and several people wished for a larger mug that would hold a proper pot of tea. He wrote it all in his notebook, for there was a next goal somewhere in all that information.

Two sisters in matching sunhats stopped at the stall and each chose a blue mug, explaining that the colour reminded them of the sea in the town where they had grown up. Kofi wrapped the mugs in paper and tied them with string, his hands steadier now, and they walked away arguing cheerfully about which was prettier. Three boxes on his card were filled, and the square had begun to hum.

A tall man in a faded jacket approached the stall near eleven o'clock and explained that it was his wife's birthday and that she adored things made by hand. He picked up three mugs in turn, held each at arm's length with the seriousness of a jeweller, and finally chose a blue one with a particularly smooth handle. Kofi found himself explaining how the handle had been pulled, and the man listened as though to a story.

At noon Hannah, a potter who had the next stall along and a long, patient face, wandered over, studied the mugs closely and bought a green one. She told him that in her own first year she had sold only three pieces, all to relatives, and that everything since had been earned by small improvements. It was said so kindly that Kofi did not mind the comparison, and he wrote down her advice about making the handles slightly longer.

At lunchtime Tomas, Lena and Joy arrived together, the baker in a suit and the student in paint-stained dungarees, and the sight of them behind the stall made Kofi's throat tighten. Lena bought a blue mug and held it up to the light, and Joy bought a green one, saying with a smile that she would use it every day and tell her students where it came from. Tomas, who already owned one, simply stood at the back with his arms folded and beamed like a man whose own son had won a prize.

In the middle of the afternoon the clouds that the forecast had promised finally opened, and a brisk shower sent the crowd running for cover. Kofi rigged the old green tarp above the stall in three minutes, exactly as Ana had taught him, and a small crowd of dripping shoppers gathered under it to wait out the rain. Four of them, to his delighted surprise, bought mugs while they waited, and the rain drummed on the tarp like applause.

At four o'clock the bell rang, the stallholders began to fold their tables and the golden light of late afternoon fell across the wet cobbles. Kofi sat on his stool and counted the money in the shoebox, then the filled boxes on his card, and the two totals agreed: eleven mugs sold at the market, nine left in the boxes. His legs were stiff, his face ached from smiling and he had never been so tired or so happy.

That night, tired and glowing, Kofi copied the market card onto the chart on the bathroom mirror and counted the filled boxes with his finger. Sixteen were black and four were still empty, and the calendar in the next room reminded him that three days remained until the thirtieth of June. He lay awake for a long time, doing the sums over and over, as accountants will.

On Sunday morning Kofi decided that a goal this close deserved a final push, and he sat down to write to everyone he could think of: friends, cousins, old classmates and neighbours. He kept each message short and honest, saying that he had made the mugs himself and that he was four short of a goal, and asking whether anyone would like one this week. Then, after a long moment spent staring at the screen, he gathered his courage and pressed send.

Dan shared a photograph of the mugs among his friends with a fine flourish of enthusiasm, and replies came in all afternoon, most of them admiring and none of them urgent. Two people said that they would certainly buy one next month, a third wanted a bigger mug and a fourth wanted to know whether he took cards. By Monday morning nobody had paid, and Kofi began to suspect that the finish line was beyond reach.

On Monday Kofi asked around the office with a pounding heart, and the results were quickly discouraging. Priya had already bought two mugs, another colleague had bought one the week before, and everyone else politely explained that their cupboards were full. To his own surprise, he took the news calmly, reasoning that a plan which had asked for sixteen people in six months had never promised that the seventeenth would appear in three days.

On the evening of the thirtieth of June, Kofi stood in front of the bathroom mirror and looked at the chart for the last time as a goal rather than a record. Sixteen boxes were filled and four were empty, and no message, no visit and no bargain could change that before midnight. He read the sentence at the top, which now described something that he had not quite done, and felt the disappointment arrive, heavy and quite sharp.

Ana arrived at his door as the clock struck ten, carrying a flask and two cups on a tray, and she looked at him and the chart without a single word of false comfort. A missed target, she said, is data and not a verdict, and she asked him to study it as a scientist would, with curiosity and without shame. She sat down at the table without being asked, uncapped the flask and poured two cups of steaming tea.

Ana drew two columns on a clean sheet and asked Kofi to fill them in with ruthless honesty. Under what worked he wrote his five weekly hours, the Sunday reviews, the batches and the support of his friends, and under what did not work he put the week of flu, the cracked batch and a slow start. The second column, to his great relief, was shorter than he had feared, and rather more interesting.

As he studied the columns, Kofi noticed something that made him sit up: the cracked batch had cost him exactly four mugs, which was precisely the size of his gap. Had the kiln been kind, he would have reached twenty with a little to spare, and the sale of five mugs to friends and colleagues had also worked far better than he had ever hoped. It was a lesson with numbers in it, and numbers, as an accountant, he could respect and learn from.

Ana reminded him where he had stood on the first of January, in a courtyard with a wish that was five years old and a lump of clay on his shelf that had turned to stone. Now he had sixteen real sales, a real skill and a plan that had held through flu, fatigue and cracking. A goal that is nearly reached, she said, has still carried you a very long way from where you started, and four short of twenty was not the same as nothing.

Before Ana left, Kofi fetched the Lessons sheet from the wall and added four fresh lines in his neatest hand: begin earlier, keep a larger cushion, make bigger mugs for tea drinkers and sell in more places. Ana read them over his shoulder and said that these were not the notes of a man who had failed. He pinned the sheet back up and, for the first time in a week, he slept soundly.

In the first week of July, Kofi took a clean sheet of paper and wrote at the top: I will sell forty mugs that I made myself before the thirty-first of December, helped by a small online page. He pinned it on the wall beside the old sheet, and the two of them looked like a pair of mountains, the smaller one standing proudly in front of the larger. Goals, he realised, could be built one upon another, each stage standing firmly on the stage before it.

Ana went through the new goal line by line with her pencil, asking the same questions that had once been so painful. Was it specific, could it be counted, did it carry a date and had he found the reason behind it? To his quiet satisfaction Kofi could answer each one in turn, and the whole exercise took twenty minutes instead of a month.

Kofi paused over the number and asked whether forty was a stretch or a break. In the first six months he had sold sixteen while still learning to centre clay, but now he had skill and a routine, so about one and a half mugs a week seemed hard but possible. It was neither a hill nor a mountain, but a climb with a real summit.

Kofi drew a new timeline backward from the thirty-first of December, and where the first one had taken a month of puzzlement, this took a single evening. The stages were clear: make the mugs in earlier and larger batches, photograph them well, open the online page in September and visit at least two more markets before Christmas. He pinned the last note in place and felt, for the first time, like a seasoned old hand at the whole business.

One of the new milestones was an online page, and Kofi approached it with the thoroughness of an accountant. He set up a white sheet and a lamp on the kitchen table and photographed each mug from four angles, since a stranger who cannot hold a mug must at least see its handle, its rim and its glaze. The pictures were not perfect, but they were honest, and he thought that honesty would sell mugs.

Kofi found that his reason had grown during the six months, and that the old card no longer said everything. He remembered Tomas drinking his tea from the green mug and the photograph that Abena had sent from her table, and he wrote a second card saying that he wanted to see people use the things he made. He propped it next to the first, where the two cards leaned against each other.

One afternoon Kofi opened the kitchen drawer and found the eight strips from the first of January lying among the batteries, a little curled at the edges. He read each in turn, remembering the pang with which he had put the marathon away, and decided that they could keep waiting a while longer, though not for ever. The rabbits were still in their hutches, and he was grateful that none had escaped.

One evening Ana pointed to the photograph of a snowy summit that hung above her kitchen table, and for the first time in his hearing she told him the story behind it. Years earlier she had led a group within a few hours of the top when the sky began to change, and she had decided, against every wish in her own body, to turn them around. They had never reached that summit, and she had never once regretted the decision, not even on the clearest evenings that followed.

The secret, Ana explained, was that she had decided the turn-around time weeks earlier, in the calm of the valley, with a clear head and a cup of tea. A person standing tired and breathless a few hours from the top is the worst possible judge of whether to continue, and so a good guide makes the rule early and obeys it later. A goal, she said, is a reason to climb and never a reason to ignore the sky.

Kofi asked himself what a turn-around rule might look like for a man with a mug goal and a full-time job, and he wrote his answer at the bottom of the new sheet. He would take one whole day of rest each week, with no clay and no spreadsheets, and if he was exhausted for three weeks in a row he would cut back his hours. Ana read it over his shoulder and said that a good goal always carries a safe way to stop, just as a good climb carries a safe way down.

On a warm evening in late summer, Kofi stood in front of the shelf and looked at the blue and green mugs lined up in the last of the sun. Eight months earlier he had owned a wish, a stiff-spined book and a lump of clay gone to stone, and now he had a skill, a plan and mugs sitting in other people's kitchens. It seemed to him that the distance between those two evenings was larger than the distance he had walked on any ordinary day.

Kofi took the paper strips out of the drawer and spread them across the table beside the first goal sheet, the tally chart and the yellowing timeline. Together they told a story that no single page could tell, of a cloud made definite, a flag planted and a route walked, one dated camp at a time. He noticed that the sheet had stopped looking like a plan and begun to look like a record.

Kofi took a clean sheet and began to write down what he had learned, beginning with the lessons that had come first and seemed, now, the simplest. Choose one goal and put the rest in a drawer, make it clear enough to count and to check, and find a reason that would matter even if nobody ever noticed. Everything else, he saw, was built on top of those three foundations, like a house upon its stones.

The next lessons concerned the plan and the long middle, and Kofi wrote them as quickly as he had lived them. Give the goal a date, plan backward from the finish in stages, prepare for the obstacles, protect the hours, check your progress every week and treat every setback as information and not as a verdict. He signed the sheet at the bottom, as if it were a small contract with the man he would be next year.

Kofi carried a small paper bag across the courtyard and knocked on Ana's door, with the faintly ridiculous nervousness of a man giving a prize. Inside the bag was his very first mug, the lopsided blue one from February with the small handle and the uneven rim, which he had never sold and never intended to. Ana looked at it for a long time, and then, with great gravity, she said that it was exactly the right size for tea.

Ana filled the lopsided mug with tea and the two of them sat by her window, watching the evening settle over her pots of herbs. After a while she admitted, with a small embarrassed laugh, that even a retired guide has a wish of her own, a very old one that she had carried for decades without ever once attaching a date. She had spent her life teaching other people to put flags on clouds, and had forgotten to plant her own.

Ana unfolded a worn map of a long coastal path that wound for several hundred miles along cliffs and bays, and she rested a finger on its start. She had wanted to walk the whole of it since she was a girl, she said, but there had always been another group to guide, another season, another reason, and now the word someday had worn quite thin. It was a pleasure to see her look, for once, like a beginner standing at the bottom of an enormous hill.

Kofi smiled, because he knew exactly what to do, and he slid a pencil and a clean sheet of paper across the table. Bring a pencil, he said, repeating the words that she had once spoken to him in the courtyard, and by dinner we will have turned your wish into a goal. Ana laughed so loudly that the herbs on the windowsill seemed to tremble, and then she picked up the pencil and wrote a date.

That night Kofi pinned a clean sheet of paper beside the tally chart on his wall, while the mugs stood in a long row on the windowsill and the courtyard lights glowed below. The sheet was empty, and he did not yet know what he would write on it, but for the first time in his life that thought was not frightening in the least. He knew how to turn a wish into a goal, and everything else was only a matter of time.

Here is the whole lesson in a few lines: choose a single goal that matters, make it specific and countable, and give it a reason and a date. Break it into stages, plan for the obstacles, check your progress every week, and treat every setback as information rather than a verdict. Then begin today, because a goal that sticks is simply a wish that someone decided to take seriously.
